title: Year two close: the book is a person
hookLine: a whole Bible in order, and the Church's year; Catholics say every page points to Christ
tomorrow: Year three opens: the story after Acts

lines: MOSES AND THE PROPHETS, MILE AFTER MILE.
cards: On the evening of the first Easter, two disciples are walking from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus, sixty furlongs, Luke says, of dust and disappointment.
A stranger falls in beside them and asks what they're talking about. They tell him everything: the hopes, the cross, the strange report of an empty tomb.

And the stranger, instead of comforting them, starts at the beginning of their own scriptures and walks them through it, Moses and the prophets, mile after mile. Later they'll say their hearts were burning.

teach.h: FROM GENESIS TO THE SEVEN BOOKS.
teach.b: Luke says it in one sentence, in the Douay-Rheims: "And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded to them in all the scriptures, the things that were concerning him."
Catholics take that verse as the key to reading the whole Bible, and it's the road this year has walked.

First, the beginning: Genesis, a garden, a flood, Abraham's tent, Joseph forgiving his brothers; then out of Egypt, the sea, the mountain, the law; then the kings, the prophets, the wisdom books, and the seven books found in Catholic Bibles, from Tobit to the Maccabees.
Second, the Gospels: Luke's mercy, then John's signs and his Word made flesh.
Third, the Church on the move: Acts, Paul's letters from Romans to Philemon, Hebrews and James, Peter, John and Jude, and the Apocalypse with its new heaven and new earth.
Fourth, the year of feasts, from Advent to Christ the King, and this last week: Friday, Saturday, Sunday and your own name.

teach.h: THE THINGS THAT WERE CONCERNING HIM.
teach.b: Saint Augustine put that reading in a pair of lines: the New Testament lies hidden in the Old, and the Old is made plain in the New.

Saint Jerome, who translated the Bible into Latin, said it more sharply: not to know the scriptures is not to know Christ. For Catholics, the Bible isn't finally a book of rules or a book of history, though it holds both.
It's a long way of meeting someone. And on that road, the disciples knew the stranger at last when he broke the bread. Tomorrow, year three: the story after Acts, the long history of the Church.

how: Catholics hear the whole sweep of scripture read at Mass through the Church's year, and the Church encourages personal reading too, often slowly, as in lectio divina, with the Gospels at the center.

games.q: you're walking to Emmaus with a stranger who has explained the scriptures the whole way. it's getting dark. what do you do?
o: ask him to stay and eat with you.
run back to Jerusalem at once.
games.why: they press him to stay. at table he breaks the bread, they know him, and he vanishes. then they run back to Jerusalem.

practice: Let this year's books pass by as they come: a garden, a burning bush, a psalm, a prodigal son walking home, a Samaritan woman at a well, a shipwreck, a letter, a city coming down from heaven.
Notice which one tugs at you, and don't argue with it; that's the book you keep, a few verses at a time. If you pray, ask to recognize him in it.

wordCard.voice: Emmaus. The village the two disciples were walking to on Easter evening, when a stranger opened the whole of scripture to them. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: word — John's name for Christ, the Word made flesh.

carryVoice: Your line: the book is a person. Two years on the road, and the stranger has a name. Year two, done.
